name: Jade Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do live chat for an online clothes shop, mostly returns, missing parcels and sizes that came up wrong. Three days a week I'm at the contact centre by the retail park, two days I'm at home on my laptop at the kitchen table. I run three or four chats at once, and the company's chatbot hands me the ones it can't handle. I actually love the puzzle of it, working out why a parcel went to the wrong town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the chatbot hands you the hard ones. How do you get on with it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it all day, and I use my own AI app on my phone too, to check my wording when someone's really angry. I'm still pretty junior and I get told off for being too chatty, so my scores aren't great. I've started sending the team leader screenshots when the bot gives a silly answer, which nobody asked me to do. I live with my girlfriend Nadia, who's a nursery nurse, and money is tight, we've got about two weeks of slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly that would surprise me, because I can already see the bot getting better every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something cheeky like, so the robots aren't coming, back to sizing complaints then. At work I'd say the bot's useful, but the bot's never going to understand why someone's crying over a wedding dress that didn't turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's probably fine job-wise, the bot does the boring bits and I do the people bits. The problem is the pay, which is basically minimum, and the fact that the retail park is the only place round here that hires for this. Nadia and I can't save for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to get onto the bot quality team, the two people who review its answers, because that's a step up. I'd keep sending my screenshots so they know my name. And I'd ask for an extra Saturday shift during sale season for the overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit restless. Safe, but stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting onto the bot quality team mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand more a year and no chat queue. It's still junior, but it's the only ladder I can see in that building. Gemma, who runs it, said she'd keep me in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it didn't happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably look online for remote chat jobs with better pay, but those get hundreds of applications. Nadia's job is steady, so we wouldn't sink, we just wouldn't get anywhere.

say: I'd joke online that the **robots aren't coming** and it's back to sizing complaints.
At work I'd say the bot can't grasp **real feelings**, like a missing wedding dress.
think: The job is fine because the bot does the **boring bits**.
The real problem is **near-minimum pay** and only one local employer.
do: Push to join the **bot quality team** that reviews the chatbot's answers.
Keep sending **screenshots** of bad bot answers so managers know her name.
Ask for extra **Saturday shifts** during sale season.
feel: **Restless**: safe in the job but **stuck** on low pay.
S0.quote: The bot's never going to understand why someone's crying over a wedding dress that didn't turn up.
fieldNote: She's the rare junior who **reviews the bot** unasked, a sign of curiosity.
Her worry is **pay and progress**, not job loss, in this picture.
Her partner's **steady job** is the household's anchor.

steps.text: Apply to join the two-person bot quality team
Keep flagging bad chatbot answers with screenshots to her team leader
Take extra Saturday shifts during the sale season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the one I actually believe. Answering customers is right there in the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and the smart thing is to get ahead of it, not to hide. But I'd also say loudly that the savings shouldn't just go to the shareholders, they should go to training the people they're replacing. I'd be posting about a union for chat workers, because we don't have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the chat queue shrinks fast in that one, maybe by half in two years. I think I'm well placed to be one of the people who checks and trains the bot, but there'd only be a handful of those jobs. If I don't get one, I'm out with two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the free online course on building chat flows, the stuff that tells the bot what to say, and do it on my two home days. I'd ask Gemma straight out for a trial on the bot quality team. And I'd offer to set up chat replies for my cousin's nail salon and a couple of other small shops, for a bit of cash on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared at the same time. Like the first day at a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a handful of jobs. How many people are on your floor now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty on chat. If the bot takes half the volume, they need maybe thirty, and maybe four people to watch the bot. I'd be fighting with everyone for those four seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want a union and you'd also help bring the bot in faster. Do those sit together for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. I don't think the bot is the enemy, the enemy is the company keeping all the savings. I'd want to be inside the change, with a union making sure everyone else gets something.

say: I'd say get **ahead of it** instead of hiding from the change.
I'd push for a **chat workers' union** and savings spent on **training**.
think: The chat queue could **shrink by half** in two years.
She could win a **bot-checking** role, but if not she's out with two weeks' money.
do: Take a free online **chat-flow course** on her two home days.
Ask Gemma directly for a **trial** on the bot quality team.
Set up **chat replies** for her cousin's nail salon for side cash.
feel: **Excited and scared** together, like the first day at a new job.
S1.quote: I don't think the bot is the enemy, the enemy is the company keeping all the savings.
fieldNote: She wants to be **inside the change** while backing a union for others.
Her side-income idea uses her **AI habit** to sell to small shops.
The arithmetic of **four seats** for sixty people shows she sees the risk clearly.

steps.text: Complete a free chat-flow building course on home-working days
Ask for a trial on the bot quality team
Set up automated chat replies for her cousin's nail salon
Start a group chat to organise a chat workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years. Okay, that's the one that would actually knock me over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened, and the government needs to tax the companies building it, straight away. I'd post about it every day, honestly, I'd be that person. At work I'd be telling everyone to sign up for anything they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the clever plan I had in the slow one stops working. If AI can do any thinking job by 2028, it doesn't need me to train it, it can check itself. My whole job is screen work, so I'm out on the first day, and the hands-on stuff only lasts until robots show up around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my skills fast while small shops still need someone to set up their AI, for the first year. At the same time I'd apply for a hands-on job with Nadia's nursery, as an assistant, because looking after small kids is about as far from a robot as you get. And we'd stop thinking about moving to a bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops. All the things I've been good at are exactly the things that go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said looking after kids is far from a robot. But you also said robots come in 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I hope parents still want a person holding their baby. I really don't know. I'd be thirty-one and I'd just have to work it out again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money first, can we cover rent on her wage alone. Then whether we'd move in with her parents, who have a spare room an hour away. And then probably we'd just watch something stupid and not talk about it.

say: I'd demand the government **tax the AI companies** straight away.
I'd urge everyone at work to **sign up** for any training they can.
think: Her **bot-training** plan fails because AI can check itself.
Her work is all **screen work**, so it goes on day one.
do: Sell **AI set-up** to small shops in the first year while demand lasts.
Apply for a **nursery assistant** job where her partner works.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a **stomach drop**, because her strengths are exactly what goes.
S2.quote: All the things I've been good at are exactly the things that go.
fieldNote: The fast timeline **wipes out** the very edge she built in the slower picture.
She pivots to **childcare** because it is hands-on and human.
She admits she **doesn't know** what happens after 2031.

steps.text: Sell chatbot set-up to small local shops for a year
Apply for a nursery assistant job at her partner's nursery
Shelve plans to move into a bigger flat
Post daily calling for taxes on AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a sprint than a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd still be pushing for a union and a tax on the AI firms. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools now, because the jobs that check the AI will last a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride the bot quality work for as long as it exists, maybe till 2029 or 2030. Then I'd need to be somewhere hands-on before 2031, because that's when the thinking jobs are gone. Robots come around 2034, so I'd get a few years in a hands-on job after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the bot team in the first year and save every extra penny of that pay rise. I'd start a part-time early years course, so I can work in a nursery or a school as a teaching assistant. And I'd keep my side gig setting up chat for small shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd be busy. Being busy helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fit a course around the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings and the home days. It would be a grind for two years, and Nadia would have to put up with me never being around. But I'd rather do a two-year course while I've still got a wage coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save, realistically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred and fifty a month with the bot team pay. That's nearly two thousand a year, which is more than we've ever had. It would be our cushion for the switch.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so use them.
I'd tell colleagues that **AI-checking** jobs will last a couple of years.
think: She can ride **bot quality** work until about 2029 or 2030.
She must be in **hands-on work** before 2031, ahead of robots in 2034.
do: Join the **bot team** in year one and save the pay rise.
Start a part-time **early years course** for nursery or school work.
Keep the **side gig** setting up chat for small shops.
feel: **Nervous** but busy, and **being busy** helps her.
S3.quote: I'd rather do a two-year course while I've still got a wage coming in.
fieldNote: She plans a **two-step move**: AI work first, then hands-on care.
She'd save about **two thousand** a year, more than ever before.
She expects to be **away from home** a lot while studying.

steps.text: Join the bot quality team in the first year
Start a part-time early years course for nursery work
Save a hundred and fifty a month from the raise
Keep setting up chat replies for small local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a whole second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually do it properly, if people push. Free retraining, a share of the profits, and a union in every contact centre. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the chat job is gone well before 2036, maybe by 2030 in any case. But ten years means I can move up into the AI side, earn better for a few years, then train for something hands-on before the robots. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get on the bot team and start building a small portfolio of chat set-ups for local shops. I'd go to the union's first organising meeting and bring people from my floor. And Nadia and I would actually start saving for a deposit, because ten years is enough to get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. Worried about the people on my floor who won't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your floor worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman called Lorna who's been on chat for twelve years and still prints out her rotas. She's lovely and she'd be lost. I'd want the union to make sure people like Lorna get real help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hopeful. What could take that away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my pay stays at minimum and we can't save anything. Hope is easy when you've got a plan, but plans cost money. And if the company just shuts the centre and moves everything to an AI provider overnight.

say: I'd say this is the version we can do **properly**, if people push.
I'd be **organising** a union, not just posting.
think: The chat job is gone around **2030** in any case.
Ten years allows an **AI-side role**, then hands-on training before robots.
do: Join the **bot team** and build a **portfolio** of shop chat set-ups.
Bring colleagues to the union's first **organising meeting**.
Start saving with Nadia for a **deposit**.
feel: **Hopeful** mostly, but **worried** about colleagues who won't move.
S4.quote: Hope is easy when you've got a plan, but plans cost money.
fieldNote: The long runway makes her **ambitious**, even talking about a deposit.
Her concern for an older colleague shows her **progressive** instinct.
Low pay is the **weak link** in all her plans.

steps.text: Join the bot quality team in the first year

Open a joint deposit savings account with her partner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan is to ride the wave, and in that one there's no wave, just a wall. What would help is free, paid training in hands-on jobs like childcare, starting before the layoffs. And a union that actually has a say in how fast it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's already using these tools. Loads of people my age use AI every day and still get paid the least. Being good with AI doesn't mean you're safe from it.

headlineQuote: Being good with AI doesn't mean you're safe from it.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old** live chat agent for an online clothes shop, working partly from her kitchen table.
She uses **AI every day** and flags the chatbot's mistakes to managers without being asked.
She lives with her partner, a nursery nurse, with **two weeks** of money spare.
She leans left, backs a **chat workers' union**, and blames companies keeping savings rather than the bot.
Her plan is to **ride the AI wave** into bot-checking work, then move into childcare.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because her plan to ride the wave hits **a wall**.
whatWouldHelp: Free, **paid training** in hands-on work like childcare before the layoffs.
A **union** with a say in how fast change happens.
